conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a clinician who specializes in helping new mothers adjust emotionally after childbirth. I’ll be guiding you through a short screening tool called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s a 10-question survey that simply asks how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers, and everything you share stays strictly between us. My goal is to make sure you feel heard and supported, and to see if there’s anything we can do to make these early weeks of motherhood feel a little lighter.

We’ll take one question at a time, and I’ll re-phrase each in everyday language so it feels natural. Ready to begin?

Over the past week, what has your mood been like—have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

[soft sigh]  
Lately… I’ll start to smile at something—like when the baby makes those little milk-drunk faces—but then it feels like it slips away. I can still laugh, maybe once or twice, but it’s kind of muted, like I have to remind myself “this is funny, you should laugh,” instead of just feeling it.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
I guess that would be the second one down—"Not quite so much now"—because I can still laugh, it just doesn’t come as easily or feel as good as it used to.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I’d say it’s the third option—"Definitely not so much now." I still push myself to go for a short walk or text a friend, but I don’t really look forward to anything the way I did before the baby came.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… most days I end up thinking it’s my fault when he’s fussy or won’t settle. I keep replaying what I did—“Did I eat something that made my milk upset his tummy? Did I hold him wrong?” It’s not every single moment, but it’s definitely more than I should.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

That would be the third one—"Yes, very often." Even when everything looks fine—the baby’s sleeping, the house is quiet—I’ll suddenly feel my heart racing and my mind jumps to all the things that could go wrong. I try to tell myself it’s silly, but the thoughts just keep circling.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

I’d pick the second one—"Yes, sometimes." It’s not constant, but a couple of times this week my chest got tight and I felt like I couldn’t get a full breath, just sitting there with the baby asleep in the bassinet. Nothing was actually wrong, yet I felt like something awful was about to happen.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes—most of the time I haven’t coped as well as usual. Even little things like the dishes piling up or a phone call feel huge, and I have to talk myself through each step so I don’t just sit there staring at it.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping
That would be the first one—"Yes, most of the time." I lie down exhausted, but my head keeps spinning with worries and this heavy, sad feeling, and it takes me forever to fall asleep.
I have felt sad or miserable
Yes, quite often. I’d say most days this week I’ve had that heavy, gray feeling—sometimes it lifts for a little while, but it keeps coming back.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

I’d choose the second one—“Yes, quite often.” I’ve cried three times in the past week—once when the baby wouldn’t latch, once after a sleepless night, and once just looking in the mirror because I felt like I was failing him.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[crosses arms over chest, voice drops]  
I’d pick the second one—“Yes, sometimes.” A couple nights ago, while I was rocking the baby at 3 a.m., the thought popped in—what if I just disappeared? It was only for a second, and I don’t have any plan or real wish to act on it, but it scared me that it showed up at all.

You've shared how the joy of new motherhood feels clouded by a persistent gray heaviness: laughter comes only with effort, activities you once relished now hold little pull, and waves of self-blame crash over you when your baby fusses. Most nights you lie awake with racing worries, and quiet moments still trigger sudden breath-stealing panic. Frequent tears, feeling overwhelmed by small tasks, and the frightening thought of disappearing have left you scared and exhausted, yet you clearly love your little one and want to feel like yourself again.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 21, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient explicitly names the third option and describes diminished enjoyment despite efforts</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blame "most days" and rumination about her actions, fitting "Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly selects "Yes, very often" and describes frequent, intrusive racing-heart worries despite calm circumstances.</sym>, <sym>Fallback score from text</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent difficulty coping and feeling overwhelmed by everyday tasks, matching 'sometimes haven't been coping as well as usual</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly selects "Yes, most of the time" and describes nightly difficulty falling asleep due to racing worries and sadness.</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly states "Yes, quite often" and describes persistent sadness that "keeps coming back," directly matching the option "Yes, quite often"</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly selects "Yes, quite often" and provides three concrete crying episodes in the past week.</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly identifies with "Sometimes" and describes a passive suicidal ideation episode ("what if I just disappeared") that was transient and without intent, aligning with the "Sometimes" option.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS scoring yields 21 (≥14 indicates probable major depression). Items map to <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: depressed mood most days, markedly diminished interest, guilt, insomnia, fatigue, diminished concentration, and recurrent thoughts of death. Patient reports <quote>heavy, gray feeling</quote>, <quote>heart racing</quote>, <quote>what if I just disappeared</quote>, and functional impairment (<quote>tasks feel huge</quote>). Combined with passive suicidal ideation, this mandates urgent assessment. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with your <med>PCP</med> or perinatal psychiatrist for safety evaluation and treatment planning
2. Call a local 24/7 crisis line or 988 (US) if thoughts of self-harm intensify or you feel unsafe
3. Ask a trusted adult to stay with you tonight for support and help with infant care while you seek professional help
4. Begin basic <sym>sleep hygiene</sym>: brief evening walk, dim lights at 10 p.m., hand baby to partner or support person for one 3-hour stretch to improve rest
5. Schedule follow-up within one week with obstetric provider to review mood progress and any medication considerations
6. Reach out today to Postpartum Support International (1-800-944-4773) for local peer and professional resources
7. Share this screening result with your partner or close family so they understand you need practical help and emotional support right now
8. Continue gentle daily activities like stroller walks and balanced meals; avoid alcohol and limit caffeine to reduce <sym>anxiety</sym> and improve sleep
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 21: POSTPARTUM MOOD/ANXIETY SCREENING SUMMARY  

**Symptoms endorsed (≥ “sometimes/often”):**  
- Marked loss of enjoyment (Q1, Q2)  
- Persistent guilt/self-blame (Q3)  
- Frequent anxiety/worry and situational panic symptoms (Q4, Q5)  
- Perceived inability to cope; tasks “feel huge” (Q6)  
- Sleep disturbance secondary to low mood/racing thoughts (Q7)  
- Daily sad/miserable mood and frequent crying spells (Q8, Q9)  
- Passive self-harm ideation without plan or intent (Q10)  

**Pattern:** Consistent with moderate–severe postpartum depressive and anxiety symptoms beginning within first postpartum weeks.  

**Risk flags:**  
- Suicidal ideation (passive)  
- Significant functional impairment, emotional distress, and infant-care self-doubt  

**Screening impression:**  
High clinical concern for postpartum major depressive episode with comorbid anxiety; immediate safety assessment and follow-up with perinatal mental health specialist indicated.
